Hierarchical Neural ODE over multiple pedons (Pillar 2 × Pillar 5)

Source: R/piml_hierarchical.R
piml_hierarchical_fit.Rd

Fits a covariate-conditioned Neural ODE \(dy/dz = f_\theta(z, y, \mathbf{x})\) jointly across every pedon in a long-format data frame, plus a sibling MLP \(y_0(\mathbf{x})\) that predicts the surface value from covariates. The two nets share the optimiser so training sees all pedons at once.

Usage

piml_hierarchical_fit(
  pedons,
  id_col,
  depth_col,
  value_col,
  covariate_cols,
  hidden = c(32L, 16L),
  y0_hidden = c(16L),
  n_steps = 4L,
  epochs = 500L,
  lr = 0.01,
  seed = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Arguments

pedons

Data frame in long form (one row per horizon) with columns for pedon id, depth, value, and one or more covariates.

id_col, depth_col, value_col

Character, column names.

covariate_cols

Character vector, names of covariate columns. Assumed constant within a pedon — the first row of each pedon is used.

hidden

Integer vector, MLP widths for the ODE vector field \(f_\theta\).

y0_hidden

Integer vector, MLP widths for the surface-value head \(y_0(\mathbf{x})\).

n_steps

Integer, RK4 steps between successive observation depths.

epochs, lr

Integer and numeric — Adam hyperparameters.

seed, verbose

As elsewhere in edaphos.

Value

A edaphos_piml_hierarchical object (S3).

Details

Once fitted, piml_hierarchical_predict() returns a profile for any new location given its covariates — no horizon measurement required. Pair with al_physics_gate_piml_hierarchical() to use that per-location envelope as a rejection filter inside the Active Learning loop.

What the piml_ prefix does and does not mean here

Despite the prefix, this function shares the family name with piml_profile_fit() and not its physics. There, the depth function IS the closed-form solution of a stated equation and the four fitted numbers are that equation's symbols. Here, \(f_\theta\) is an unconstrained multi-layer perceptron taking \((z, y, \mathbf{x})\) as input channels; the covariates do not enter as \(\lambda_0(\mathbf{x})\), \(\mu(\mathbf{x})\), \(y_\infty(\mathbf{x})\), and no conservation law or monotonicity constrains the result.

Two consequences follow and neither is hypothetical. The state can cross zero, so a strictly positive property can be predicted negative — see the clamp argument of piml_hierarchical_predict(). And the fitted parameters are not interpretable as rates or asymptotes, so none of the identifiability results reported for piml_profile_fit_bayesian() carry over. Treat this as a flexible depth-profile regressor conditioned on covariates, which is what it is.

Examples

# torch is a Suggests dependency AND the lantern binaries are a
# separate download, so both halves of the guard are needed.
if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&
    isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {
  data(br_cerrado)

  # Five Cerrado sites.  Each pedon is the noise-free closed-form
  # solution of dy/dz = -lambda0 exp(-mu z) (y - y_inf) with
  # lambda0 = 0.02 + 0.004 twi, mu = 0.02 and y_inf = 0.30 y0, so
  # the covariates genuinely drive the shape of the profile.
  sites <- br_cerrado[c(1, 400, 900, 1400, 1900), ]
  hz <- c(5, 15, 30, 60)
  pedons <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(i) {
    y0   <- sites$soc[i]
    lam0 <- 0.02 + 0.004 * sites$twi[i]
    data.frame(pedon = paste0("P", i), depth = hz,
               soc = 0.30 * y0 + 0.70 * y0 *
                     exp(-(lam0 / 0.02) * (1 - exp(-0.02 * hz))),
               twi = sites$twi[i], ndvi = sites$ndvi[i],
               map_mm = sites$map_mm[i])
  }))

  # 20 epochs, not the 500 of the default, to keep this short.
  # `seed` seeds torch, so the loss below is reproducible.
  fit <- piml_hierarchical_fit(
    pedons, "pedon", "depth", "soc",
    covariate_cols = c("twi", "ndvi", "map_mm"),
    epochs = 20L, lr = 0.05, n_steps = 2L, seed = 1L)
  print(fit)

  # `final_loss` is an MSE in standardised units, so the number it
  # has to beat is the loss of predicting the global mean of `soc`.
  vn <- (pedons$soc - mean(pedons$soc)) / sd(pedons$soc)
  print(round(c(global_mean = mean(tapply(vn^2, pedons$pedon, mean)),
                epoch_1     = fit$loss_history[1],
                final       = fit$final_loss), 4))

  # Read that final loss against the size of what produced it: two
  # MLPs, 818 weights, fitted to 20 numbers.  A five-pedon fit is an
  # interface demonstration and the loss above measures
  # memorisation, not pedology.  ?piml_hierarchical_predict holds
  # one pedon out and the model then loses to the depthwise mean of
  # the others.
  print(c(weights = sum(vapply(fit$model$parameters,
                               function(p) p$numel(), 0)),
          values  = nrow(pedons)))

  # Covariates are taken from the FIRST ROW of each pedon.  Permuting
  # them among the deeper horizons -- which leaves the column mean
  # and sd, hence the standardisation, untouched -- changes nothing,
  # while touching the topsoil row moves the loss.  So a
  # horizon-level covariate (clay of each horizon, say) is silently
  # truncated to its topsoil value.
  deep <- pedons$depth > 5
  perm <- pedons; perm$twi[deep] <- rev(perm$twi[deep])
  top  <- pedons; top$twi[!deep] <- 99
  short_fit <- function(d)
    piml_hierarchical_fit(d, "pedon", "depth", "soc",
      covariate_cols = c("twi", "ndvi", "map_mm"),
      epochs = 2L, lr = 0.05, n_steps = 2L, seed = 1L)$final_loss
  print(c(base = short_fit(pedons), deep_permuted = short_fit(perm),
          topsoil_changed = short_fit(top)))
}
